turns.text: I remember walking into my work unit that July, the walls thick with the stink of glue and ink from the big-character posters. My hands shook as I read what you and your friends wrote about our director—a man who survived the war, now called a “counterrevolutionary dog.” You wrote those words. You forced us to stand and read them aloud, again and again, until the words burned in my throat like acid. Research stopped. We weren’t allowed to touch our equipment. I watched a woman cry because her only crime was curling her hair. Children chased her, scissors in hand, shrieking, while you all laughed. My mother was seventy, forced to wear a black sash and sent away like garbage because of her family background. You made her into an enemy. When I tried to give her my ration coupons, I was told I was “covering up for a landlord.” You did this. You made us afraid in our own homes, whispering at dinner, hiding family photos, teaching children to lie. You turned suspicion into a weapon and made us use it on each other. Do you feel proud of that?

Proud? No. But I won’t lie and say I didn’t feel something powerful then—something I mistook for pride. I remember the smell of those posters too, the way the glue stuck to my fingers, how my handwriting shook at first and then steadied as I copied slogans. I thought I was writing truth, exposing hidden enemies. I believed it, because every meeting, every shout from the loudspeakers, every nod from the older students told me this was justice.

When we made you read those words, I watched your face. I saw the director’s knuckles go white, his lips pressed together. I didn’t laugh at the woman with curled hair, but I didn’t stop the others either. I did nothing when the children chased her. I remember the sound of scissors snapping, the jeers echoing down the corridor. I told myself she was showing off, that she deserved to be brought low for her vanity, her “bourgeois” habits. That’s what we were taught to see.

Your mother—people like her—were easy targets. Old, quiet, with the wrong background. I was the one who wrote her name on a list. I remember the ink smearing because my hands were sweating. I told myself this was cleansing, that the pain was necessary. When you tried to give her your coupons, I watched from the doorway as you were pulled away. I heard you cry out. I turned my back.

You say I made you afraid in your own home. Yes. I did that. I was afraid too, every night. I hid my own father’s books, cut up family photos, burned letters from relatives overseas. I taught my younger brother to recite the right slogans so he wouldn’t slip up at school. I told myself this was the only way to survive, to belong.

Now, when I think back, I see the faces—yours, your mother’s, the director’s—more clearly than the slogans. I feel shame, yes, but it’s tangled with something else: the memory of being swept up, of wanting to be safe, to be seen as pure, to have power for once. I can’t untangle it completely. I don’t expect you to forgive me. I don’t forgive myself. But pride? No. Not anymore.

You talk about shame now, but back then, you strutted through the compound like you owned it. I remember the day you and your group barged into our courtyard, banging on doors, demanding to see everyone’s household registration papers. My neighbor, a quiet widow, was dragged outside because her son had gone to Taiwan years before. You made her kneel in the mud while people spat at her. I saw you smirk as she tried to wipe her face with trembling hands. That night, I couldn’t sleep. Every footstep in the corridor made my heart race. My hands shook so badly I spilled tea on the table, and my child asked me why I was afraid. I couldn’t answer.

I started hiding my notebooks, tearing out pages with family names, burning anything that could be used against us. My son stopped playing in the courtyard—he was afraid the other children would call him “little landlord.” You made children into spies. You made parents lie to their own children, and children lie to their parents. I still wake up at night, sweating, when I hear someone shout in the street. You say you hid your father’s books. Fine. But you came into my home and made me afraid to speak, afraid to remember, afraid to hope. You destroyed trust. You destroyed us from the inside out. Did you ever think about what it means to be that afraid of your own neighbors? Or did you just enjoy the power?

You say I strutted, and maybe I did. I remember the weight of that red armband on my sleeve, the way people’s eyes flicked away as we walked into a courtyard. There was a charge in the air—fear, yes, but also a kind of twisted respect. I felt taller, louder. I remember that night, the widow in the mud. I remember her hair plastered to her cheeks, the way her knees left dark stains in the earth. I did smirk, I won’t deny it. I thought I was righteous, that I was exposing a hidden traitor’s family. I didn’t see her as a person—just a symbol, an obstacle to be cleared away. I didn’t care about her tears. I cared about not being the next one kneeling.

When I demanded household papers, I was terrified someone would ask about mine. My own father’s file was hidden in the bottom of a flour sack, and I lived in dread that someone would dig it out. I was always looking over my shoulder, always ready to accuse first so no one would point at me. That’s not an excuse, but it’s the truth: I was desperate to belong, desperate not to fall.

You talk about your son—how he stopped playing, how he learned to be silent. I saw that too, in my own family. My little brother flinched when I raised my voice. My mother stopped singing in the kitchen. I saw neighbors cross the street to avoid me. I heard children whisper “Black Five” behind other kids’ backs, and I let it happen. Sometimes I started it, because it was safer to be the one pointing than the one being pointed at.

Did I enjoy the power? Maybe, at first. It felt like safety. But it was hollow. Every time I shouted, every time I forced someone to kneel, I felt more brittle inside. The fear never left. I watched people I’d known my whole life turn away from me, and I told myself it was for the revolution. But I knew, even then, that something was breaking that couldn’t be fixed. I didn’t think about what it meant for you to be afraid of your neighbors. I only thought about what would happen if I became the target. That’s the truth.

You want to talk about truth? Here’s mine: I still flinch when I hear boots on concrete. I still check over my shoulder when I leave my apartment, even now, decades later. That’s what your “safety” cost me. I can’t trust anyone—not my colleagues, not my neighbors, not even my own family. You turned every meal into a test. We sat at the table in silence, listening for sounds outside, never knowing if you’d come again. My son stopped asking questions. He learned to keep his head down, to erase himself. He grew up afraid to speak his mind, afraid to dream. That’s on you.

I watched you drag women into the street, tie old shoes around their necks, make them confess to “crimes” that were nothing. I saw you force a girl to write her own name on a sign and hang it from her neck. She used to help my mother carry water. After that day, she never looked anyone in the eye again. You made us complicit, too—if we didn’t join in, we were next. So we clapped, or we stayed silent, or we turned away. I still taste the bile in my mouth from those afternoons.

You say you felt brittle. I wonder if you ever felt anything when you watched someone break for real. Did you sleep better knowing you were safe for one more night? Did you ever stop to think what you were making us into? I want to know if you ever looked at the faces in those crowds and realized you were destroying more than just “enemies.” You destroyed the very idea of trust. You made us strangers to ourselves. I’m still picking up the pieces.

You want to know if I felt anything when I watched someone break? I did. I remember the first time I saw a teacher collapse on the ground after we’d paraded her through the streets, her face streaked with ink and spit. I remember the way her body shook, how the crowd’s shouting faded into a low, sickening hum in my ears. My hands were still sticky from the ink bottle I’d upended on her head. I felt a knot in my stomach, but I swallowed it down and told myself she deserved it. That was the only way I could keep standing there with the others.

When we made that girl write her own name and hang it around her neck, I watched her fingers tremble as she gripped the brush. I saw my own reflection in the window behind her—my jaw clenched, my eyes hard. I told myself I was strong, that I had to be. But I remember that night, lying awake, the taste of bile in my own mouth, thinking of her face. I didn’t sleep. I stared at the ceiling and listened for footsteps, convinced someone would come for me next.

You say I destroyed trust, made you strangers to yourselves. I believe you. After the worst of it, I couldn’t look my father in the eye. He was labeled a “reactionary academic authority”—I watched him shrink, day by day, until he barely spoke at all. My mother stopped talking to neighbors. My own friends turned on me, or I turned on them first. I saw people beaten to death in the street, and I ran. I ran to Baiyangdian, thinking distance would keep the guilt off me, but it followed me everywhere. I joined the army through the back door, thinking a uniform would make me clean again. It didn’t.

I remember the violence I did with my own hands. I remember the nurse who hanged herself after we humiliated her at the hospital. I remember the teacher whose hair I shaved off with a rusted clipper, the way the scalp bled and she screamed. I remember the taste of fear and the stink of sweat and ink and burning books. I don’t sleep better. I haven’t slept well in decades. When I hear boots on concrete, I flinch too.

You’re right—I broke something in you, and in myself. I can’t put it back together either, no matter how many times I try to explain or remember. I can’t undo what I did. I can only tell you that I see those faces, every night, and I know what I destroyed.
